public_health_question.v: What does published trial evidence show about tafenoquine's efficacy and safety for malaria prophylaxis and antirelapse therapy, and how should clinicians use it?

ev.q: This report reviews evidence for the efficacy and safety of tafenoquine and provides CDC guidance for clinicians
Guidance for Using Tafenoquine for Prevention and Antirelapse Therapy for Malaria
examined the efficacy of tafenoquine in the prevention of relapse in patients with confirmed P. vivax malaria
Common adverse events included abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, vertigo, dizziness, sleep disturbances, and headache.
Based on the results of the review, CDC subject matter experts developed guidance for the use of tafenoquine.
A total of 269 articles were collated and underwent title, abstract, and full text reviews by two physicians
CDC conducted a search of English-language articles available in PubMed, Ovid Medline, Scopus, and Global Health (CABDirect)

equity.level_reason: Age only bounds the populations for which tafenoquine is approved or recommended; no social-position dimension is analyzed or framed.

ev.q: Adults aged ≥18 years can take tafenoquine (Arakoda 100 mg tablets) to prevent malaria.
Persons aged ≥16 years requiring antirelapse therapy for P. vivax or P. ovale can take tafenoquine

notes: All efficacy and safety figures (protective efficacy with CIs, chi-square, Fisher exact, log-rank tests, hazard ratios) are cited from published trials, so they are not the article's own procedures. The article's own counts are only the literature-screening tallies (269 articles, 8 included). Setting is international by trial data; the guidance itself is for the United States.
